title: A common good section for two surjections over a field
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $m,n\geq0$, and let $a,b:k^{\oplus n}\to k^{\oplus m}$ be surjective $k$-linear maps, where $k^{\oplus t}$ is the module of $t$-tuples with componentwise operations [def-weil-pbc-free-module]. There exists a $k$-linear map $q:k^{\oplus m}\to k^{\oplus n}$ such that $a\circ q=\mathrm{id}_{k^{\oplus m}}$ and $b\circ q$ is a linear isomorphism. No assumption that $k$ is infinite is imposed; empty coordinate sets are allowed.

source.place: Tag 0FJK (lemma-homotopic-surjections), final paragraph: the field common-complement assertion and its residue-field lift; details explicitly omitted in the source.

proof.text: Write $V=k^{\oplus n}$, $W=k^{\oplus m}$, $P=\ker a$, and $Q=\ker b$. The standard coordinate vectors span $V$ and $W$. Every subspace $S\subseteq V$ is finite-dimensional: choose a complement by [lem-trf-vector-subspace-complement]; projection onto $S$ along this complement is linear by uniqueness of the decomposition, and the projections of the finitely many standard vectors span $S$. Thus all subspaces used below are finite-dimensional. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-idempotent-charpoly-rank-nullity] to $a,b$. Surjectivity identifies both images with $W$, so $\dim W+\dim P=\dim V=\dim W+\dim Q$, and cancellation gives $\dim P=\dim Q$.

source.place: Tag 0FJK (lemma-homotopic-surjections), final paragraph: the field common-complement assertion and its residue-field lift; details explicitly omitted in the source.

proof.text: Set $I=P\cap Q$. Applying [lem-trf-vector-subspace-complement] inside $P$ and $Q$ gives $P=I\oplus P_1$ and $Q=I\oplus Q_1$. Projection $P\to I$ has image $I$ and kernel $P_1$; projection $Q\to I$ has image $I$ and kernel $Q_1$. By [lem-weil-pbc-idempotent-charpoly-rank-nullity], $\dim I+\dim P_1=\dim P$ and $\dim I+\dim Q_1=\dim Q$. Step 1 and cancellation give $\dim P_1=\dim Q_1$. Also $P+Q=I\oplus P_1\oplus Q_1$: generation follows by the two decompositions; if $i+x+y=0$ with $i\in I$, $x\in P_1$, $y\in Q_1$, then $y\in P\cap Q=I$, hence $y=0$, and then $i=x=0$.

source.place: Tag 0FJK (lemma-homotopic-surjections), final paragraph: the field common-complement assertion and its residue-field lift; details explicitly omitted in the source.

proof.text: By [lem-trf-equal-dimension-linear-equivalence] choose a linear isomorphism $e:P_1\to Q_1$. Let $D=\{x+e(x):x\in P_1\}\subseteq P+Q$, a subspace since $e$ is linear. If $x+e(x)\in P$, then $e(x)\in P\cap Q_1=0$, so $x=0$; hence $D\cap P=0$. If $x+e(x)\in Q$, then $x\in Q\cap P_1=0$, so $D\cap Q=0$. Moreover $P+D=P+Q$: for $y\in Q_1$ put $x=e^{-1}(y)$ and use $y=(x+e(x))-x$; the remaining $I,P_1$ lie in $P$. Similarly $Q+D=P+Q$, using $x=(x+e(x))-e(x)$ for $x\in P_1$. Thus $D$ complements both $P$ and $Q$ inside $P+Q$.

source.place: Tag 0FJK (lemma-homotopic-surjections), final paragraph: the field common-complement assertion and its residue-field lift; details explicitly omitted in the source.

proof.text: Choose a complement $R$ of $P+Q$ in $V$ using [lem-trf-vector-subspace-complement], and put $U=D+R$. Since $D\subseteq P+Q$ and $(P+Q)\cap R=0$, this sum is direct. Step 3 gives $P+U=V=Q+U$. If $d+r\in P$ with $d\in D$, $r\in R$, then $r\in(P+Q)\cap R=0$, and $d\in D\cap P=0$. The same argument with $Q$ gives $U\cap Q=0$. Consequently $V=P\oplus U=Q\oplus U$.

source.place: Tag 0FJK (lemma-homotopic-surjections), final paragraph: the field common-complement assertion and its residue-field lift; details explicitly omitted in the source.

proof.text: The restriction $a|_U:U\to W$ is injective because $U\cap\ker a=0$. It is surjective: lift $w\in W$ to $v\in V$ using the given surjectivity, write $v=p+u$ in $P\oplus U$, and obtain $a(u)=w$. The identical argument with $Q=\ker b$ shows that $b|_U$ is bijective. Define $q(w)$ to be the unique $u\in U$ with $a(u)=w$, viewed in $V$. Uniqueness and linearity of $a$ show $q(w+w')=q(w)+q(w')$ and $q(cw)=cq(w)$, so $q$ is linear and $a\circ q=\mathrm{id}_W$. Its map into $U$ is inverse to $a|_U$; hence $b\circ q$ is bijective, with inverse $a|_U\circ(b|_U)^{-1}$, which is linear by the same uniqueness argument. If $m=0$, both $q$ and the endomorphism of $W=0$ have the asserted properties; $n=0$ forces $m=0$ by surjectivity. The construction only uses addition, subtraction, and linear isomorphisms, so it also applies in characteristic $2$ and over every finite field.
